title: Manage an effective communication plan in extension and development in a simple setting

lessons.title: Building a communication plan
lessons.html:
Why a communication plan?

Extension programmes often fail not because the technology is wrong but because the right people did not hear the right message at the right time. A communication plan sets out who must be reached, with what message, through which channels, when, by whom and at what cost. Consider a provincial programme to control foot rot and internal parasites in sheep in a communal area of the Eastern Cape. Farmers, herders, the wool growers' association, the local animal health technician and the traditional council all need different information.

Components of a communication plan

  1. Situation analysis - the problem, current knowledge and practices, existing communication channels.
  2. Communication objectives - specific and measurable, for example 80 percent of registered sheep owners know the date and venue of the next treatment day.
  3. Target audiences - primary (sheep owners and herders) and secondary (traditional leaders, wool buyers, councillors).
  4. Key messages - short, clear and consistent.
  5. Channels and activities - meetings, community radio, WhatsApp groups, posters at the shearing shed, demonstrations.
  6. Timeline - aligned with the farming calendar, for example before lambing or shearing.
  7. Roles and responsibilities - who prepares, approves and delivers each item.
  8. Budget - printing, airtime, transport and venue costs in ZAR.
  9. Monitoring and evaluation - how you will know the plan worked.

Audience analysis

For each audience, record their language, literacy, preferred channels, information needs and influence on others. Herders may be young men who use cell phones and listen to radio, while owners may be older and rely on community meetings. Messages must suit each group.

lessons.title: Messages, channels and materials
lessons.html:
Designing messages

Good extension messages are:

  • Clear - one main idea.
  • Relevant - linked to what the audience cares about, such as wool income or lamb survival.
  • Actionable - say what to do: bring all sheep to the handling pens at the dip tank on Saturday morning.
  • Consistent - the same core message across all channels and partners.
  • Accurate - technically checked; product advice refers to the label or the vet.

Choosing channels

ChannelStrengthsLimits
Face-to-face meetingsTwo-way, builds trustReaches few people, costly in time
Community radioWide reach, local languageOne-way, timing matters
WhatsApp and SMSFast, cheap, remindersNeeds phones and data; rumours spread
Posters and leafletsLasting referenceNeed literacy; must be placed well
DemonstrationsSeeing is believingNeed preparation and resources

Use a mix: a radio announcement to raise awareness, a meeting to explain, a demonstration to show and SMS reminders before the event.

Developing and pre-testing materials

  1. Draft the material with input from technical experts.
  2. Translate and check with fluent speakers.
  3. Pre-test with a small group from the target audience.
  4. Revise based on what they understood or misunderstood.
  5. Get approval from your manager where required.

Working with partners

Agree on shared messages with partners such as commodity organisations, input suppliers and NGOs, so farmers do not receive conflicting advice. Agree who speaks to the media.

lessons.title: Managing, monitoring and adjusting the plan
lessons.html:
Putting the plan into action

Managing a communication plan means coordinating people, time and money so that activities happen as planned and achieve their objectives.

Implementation management

  • Keep an activity schedule with dates, responsible persons and status.
  • Hold short progress check-ins with the team and partners.
  • Track spending against the budget and keep receipts.
  • Confirm logistics before each event: venue, transport, interpreter, sound system, materials.
  • Keep a contact list of farmers, groups and media, respecting privacy and consent for messaging.

Monitoring

Collect information during implementation:

  • Outputs: number of radio slots aired, leaflets distributed, meetings held.
  • Reach: attendance at meetings, number of people in WhatsApp groups.
  • Understanding: quick checks after meetings, such as asking farmers to repeat the key message.
  • Action: number of sheep brought to treatment days compared with registered numbers.

Adjusting the plan

If attendance is low, find out why: perhaps the meeting clashed with a funeral or pension pay-out day, or the radio slot aired when herders were in the veld. Change the timing or channel. If farmers misunderstand a message, simplify it and add a demonstration. Record changes and the reasons.

Managing risks

Plan for risks such as misinformation, a disease outbreak requiring urgent messages, or a key partner withdrawing. Prepare a simple crisis communication procedure: who approves urgent messages, which channels to use and how to correct rumours quickly with accurate information from the state vet or department.

Reporting

At the end, compare results with objectives, document lessons and share a short report with partners and the community.

Key points

  • A communication plan covers audiences, objectives, messages, channels, timing, roles, budget and evaluation.
  • Analyse each audience's language, literacy and preferred channels.
  • Messages must be clear, relevant, actionable, consistent and accurate.
  • Combine channels and pre-test materials.
  • Monitor reach, understanding and action, and adjust the plan.

Repeat the same meeting at the same time
